openingMessage: If you leave this meeting knowing one more thing than you walked in with, it worked. Let's make these ten minutes count.
openingWhy: The hand who fought a frozen pump hose trying to kill a well wrote it up on his OWL form — and now every crew that reads it learns that lesson the easy way. One form reaches every trailer in the Basin by morning. What you know only protects people if it moves.
leadershipThought: Rescue capability must be staged before you ascend — someone must be able to get you down. That plan exists before the first rung. Not after.

specialFocus.title: The 30-Minute Loop — Red Flag to Decision
specialFocus.standardLabel: My Part of the Loop — Every Shift
specialFocus.why:
Look at what your own crew wrote this month. On the 12th, Stefanie Kirschke's crew got an emergency call on a leak — they treated it like an emergency, checked for gas, and kept monitoring while they worked the problem. That is the loop firing exactly the way it should: something changed, and it moved. Then look at what Jeremy Norris wrote on the 18th. Job went smooth, MT was happy — and his one thing to do better was “have a better time frame of exactly when we will be on a job when it's an unexpected call, so they're not waiting.” Read that again. Nothing went wrong on that location. The gap was that the answer never came back — somebody on the other end was standing there guessing. That's a loop that opened and didn't close.

That's what this is about. The 30-Minute Loop isn't a form and it isn't a chain of command you climb when things get bad enough. It is situational awareness plus a phone call: field to regional, regional to Canon leadership, decision back to the crew — inside thirty minutes. The reason we put a clock on it is that a surprise you sit on for two hours stops being a surprise and starts being an incident. And the reason the decision has to come back is that a crew waiting on an answer is a crew improvising. On the 11th, Stefanie's crew adjusted mid-job to a change in leadership and still finished safe — and her takeaway was to know who's responsible for the job before it starts. Same lesson. The loop is how we all know.
standard: I call when I see it, not after I've tried to solve it alone. Scope changed, gas showed up, I'm running behind, the company man's got a problem — my regional manager hears it from me first, in minutes, not at the end of the day.
No flag is too small. Nobody at Canon has ever been in trouble for making the call. Plenty of days have gone sideways because somebody decided it wasn't worth bothering anyone over.
I give the facts straight: where I am, what changed, what I need, and by when. A clear thirty-second call gets a decision. A vague one gets three more calls.

If it isn't on a ticket, it isn't a Canon job. Somebody asks me to work off the board — a favor, a side job, “don't worry about writing it up” — my answer is “let me get my regional on the phone.” I never have to be the one who says no. I just have to be the one who makes the call.
I don't let a loop die on me. If I made the call and haven't heard the decision come back, I call again. The loop isn't closed until the crew on location has the answer in hand.

scenarios.title: The Unexpected Call
scenarios.body: Short-notice call comes in — a job nobody planned for this morning. You're rolling, but you're honestly not sure whether you're forty minutes out or ninety, and you don't know what's already on that location. Run it the quiet way first: you drive, you figure you'll sort it out when you get eyes on it, and the rep on location spends an hour and a half wondering whether anybody is coming. Nothing unsafe happened — and we still lost his confidence. Now run it through the loop. Five minutes in, you call your regional: “Unexpected call, I'm on 285 north of Orla, I'll be on location by 7:40, I don't know the scope — can somebody confirm what's staged out there?” Regional gets Canon leadership, somebody calls the rep with a real ETA, and the answer comes back to you before you turn off the highway. Same drive. Same job. The difference is that nobody was standing around guessing — and that is entirely a decision you make in the first five minutes.

scenarios.title: The Side Job on the Downlow
scenarios.body:
You're wrapping up. A company man — a good one, somebody you like, somebody who's been straight with you all week — walks over and lowers his voice. “Hey, while you've got the meter out. I've got another pad about six miles up. Run over and sniff it for me real quick? Don't worry about writing it up, don't put it on the ticket. Keep it between us and I'll take care of you.”

Understand what he just handed you, because it isn't a favor. Nobody asks you to keep it quiet unless they already know it's outside the lines. Off the ticket means there is no scope, no JSA, and no permit on that pad. It means Canon doesn't know where you are — so if you go down over there, nobody comes looking, because nobody knows you're on that location. It means if something goes wrong, you're standing in it by yourself: no coverage, no paper, no company behind you, and a rep who suddenly never had that conversation. And it means the next ask is easier for him and harder for you, because now he's got something on you.

Here's the part that matters: the answer is not no. You are not the bad guy, and you don't have to turn him down. Fifteen seconds, right there in front of him: “Yes sir — let me get my regional on the phone real quick and we'll get it set up right.” Then you make the call. Nine times out of ten Canon wants that work — your regional gets it ticketed, scoped, and dispatched, and you drive over there covered, with a JSA, on the clock, and Canon bills for it. The work still gets done. The rep still gets helped. The only thing that changed is that it's on the board.

And you report it even if you already said no. Not to get anybody in trouble — if a rep is asking one of us, he's asking others, and the guy he asks next might be the newest hand we've got.

questions: Think about the last time something changed on you at a location — scope, gas, timing, a rep with a problem. Did you make the call, or did you decide you'd handle it yourself? Be honest.
When you made a call this month, did the decision actually come back to you — or did you end up guessing anyway? If it went dead, say so right now, because that's ours to fix.
Has anybody ever asked you to run something off the ticket? You're not in trouble and nobody's getting named — I need to know if it's happening out there.
What makes "let me get my regional on the phone" hard to say out loud to a company man you like? Say it here, because that hesitation is the whole problem.
What's the flag you'd hesitate to call in — the one that feels too small to bother anybody with? That's exactly the one we want.
specialFocus.nonNegotiable: See it, say it, let the loop solve it — together. Thirty minutes from red flag to decision. And no Canon hand ever works a job that isn't on the board — you don't say no, you make the call.
